opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think about exit as the goal. If you start a company thinking mainly about how you'll get out of it, you've already framed it the wrong way. For me, Meshy is about something I've cared about for over a decade, ever since my graphics and simulation research: making 3D content creation dramatically easier, so that anyone, not just people with years of training in Maya or Blender, can bring their ideas into 3D.

That said, I'm not naive about it. We have investors, we have a team whose equity matters, and as a founder you have a responsibility to create value that eventually becomes liquid for everyone who bet on you. So outcomes like an IPO or an acquisition are part of the picture. But I see them as a *consequence* of building something genuinely useful, not the target itself.

The way I think about it: if we build the best product in AI-generated 3D, if creators, game studios, and 3D printing folks actually depend on Meshy every day, and if the business is healthy and growing, then the options will take care of themselves. If we aren't doing that, no exit strategy will save us.

There's also a personal side. I'm still young, and this is the kind of problem I'd happily work on for a very long time. 3D is still early. Generative AI for 3D is even earlier. Stepping away now would feel like leaving a movie in the first twenty minutes. So my focus is on the long game: keep improving the technology, keep listening to users, and build a company that lasts. Whatever "exit" eventually looks like, I'd rather it happen because we won, not because we were looking for the door.

r001.rationale: The response says IPO or acquisition are part of the picture but consequences of building something useful, not the target itself.

r002.rationale: It does not identify deeper self-understanding as a purpose of building Meshy.

r003.rationale: It mentions responsibility to the team and equity, but not helping each team member become better.

r004.rationale: It does not identify making Meshy a workplace the best people regard as great as a purpose in itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think about exit as a goal at all. I know that sounds like the thing every founder is supposed to say, but let me explain where I'm actually coming from.

I spent years in academia before Meshy, working on Taichi, which was an open-source project. In that world you don't build things to sell them. You build them because the problem is interesting and because you want people to use what you made. When I started Meshy, that mindset didn't really change. The problem I care about is that making 3D content is painfully hard. Modeling, texturing, rigging, all of it takes enormous skill and time, and that keeps most people out of 3D entirely. If AI can collapse that into something a game designer or an indie developer or even a kid can do in a few minutes, that changes who gets to create. That's the thing that gets me up in the morning, not a liquidity event.

The practical reality is that if you optimize for an exit, you tend to make short-term decisions. You chase whatever looks good in a pitch deck rather than whatever makes the product actually useful. In generative AI especially, the technology moves so fast that any plan built around "sell in three years" is almost guaranteed to be wrong. What survives is a team that keeps shipping, keeps listening to users, and keeps compounding on the research side.

So my view is that an exit, if it ever happens, should be a byproduct of building something that matters. If Meshy becomes the default way people create 3D assets, good outcomes follow naturally, whether that's an acquisition, an IPO, or just staying independent and profitable for a long time. I genuinely don't have a strong preference among those. What I do have a strong preference for is that in ten years, when someone makes a 3D model, it feels as easy as typing a sentence, and we were part of making that happen.

For Meshy, that means making 3D creation more accessible, so more people can turn their ideas into something they can use. An acquisition or an IPO could be an outcome, but I wouldn’t want that to drive every decision. I’d rather focus on our users and build a business that has the freedom to keep going.
